newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Metro says loss probe unfounded.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Metro says loss probe unfounded.

text.p: German retail giant Metro AG on Monday brushed off news that Cologne prosecutors had opened an investigation into its plans to offset carried-over losses from its recent merger with other leading store groups.

Metro merged in July with SB-Kauf, Asko and Kaufhof to form Europe's largest unified retail group. It said in its issue prospectus the opportunity to offset carried-over losses against corporation tax would help boost the group's earnings.

But a protest lodged by a private individual, Manfred Schuermeyer, alleges Swiss-controlled Metro misled investors because the tax office had not finally approved the carrying forward of the losses, which date back to 1988.
Metro said in a statement that plans to offset 1.9 billion marks in losses from SB-Kauf had received the verbal backing of tax authorities, as stated in the prospectus.
"The board of Metro sees no reason to correct its earlier comments on this subject," the company said in a statement.
A spokeswoman for the prosecutor's office confirmed that the investigation had started but could not say when it would be completed or give any further details.
Under German law, prosecutors are obliged to examine all credible complaints.
News of the investigation, reported by Der Spiegel magazine on Monday, wiped more than six marks off the Metro share price in pre-bourse trading.
The stock recovered on the company's response to close up 3.90 marks at 130.40 marks but remained below its initial listing price of 143 marks in July.
Schuermeyer, a management consultant reached by Reuters at his office near Frankfurt, said he was "100 percent" certain the loss carry-over would be annulled as a result of the probe.
"The time span shows that the final examination of Metro's books has not yet been completed," Schuermeyer said. "Verbal assurances don't count for much."
Schuermeyer said he had been a former member of the German cooperative retail movement taken over by SB-Kauf in 1988, the year of the losses.
But neither the company nor retail analysts appeared to rate Schuermeyer's chances too highly.
Metro spokesman Hans-Joachim Wieckmann told Reuters he expected the protest to "run into the sand."
Retail analysts, meanwhile, said they did not take the protest seriously.
"This action is senseless," said retail analyst Michael Wand at Paribas in Frankfurt.
"It's rubbish," agreed Charalampos Christopoulos of BZW.
"I can't imagine that when this was one of the main reasons for the merger that management would have exposed itself in this way," Wand told Reuters.

The responsible tax authorities could not be reached for comment but with Schuermeyer convinced of the legal basis for his argument, it may be too soon to write off his lone crusade against the store conglomerate.

Swiss-controlled Metro is seeking to boost earnings by 400 million marks a year through the merger. But, battling with slow demand, it has revised down its 1996 sales forecast to 62 billion marks and said it saw no improvement next year.

Pre-tax profits are forecast between 1.0 and 1.1 billion marks ($655.7-$721.3 million) this year, and Paribas' Wand said he expected that figure to rise to 1.3 billion marks in 1997 and 1.7 billion in 1998.
